metadata.title: Atomicity: a 100 transfer is all or nothing
metadata.subject: Computer Science
metadata.objective: Show why atomicity and rollback keep a transaction's partial writes invisible.
misconceptions: A failed transaction leaves partial writes behind
Other sessions can read uncommitted rows
expectedUnderstanding: The buffer holds a staged debit of 100 on A while B has not yet been credited; that is a partial write.
The committed table is what every other session reads, and it stays at 200 and 50 while the buffer is private.
Commit applies both staged writes as one unit: A becomes 100 and B becomes 150 at the same moment.
Rollback discards the buffer and the committed values never move, so no partial state can survive.

primitives.text: Atomicity: a 100 transfer is all or nothing
In flight: A is debited to 100 in the buffer; B is not yet credited.
Other sessions read only the committed column: 200 and 50.
COMMIT: both writes become visible together.
ROLLBACK: the buffer is discarded; 200 and 50 remain.

checkpoints.title: In flight
checkpoints.body: The buffer has a staged debit on A. What does another session read for A at this moment, and why?

checkpoints.title: Commit
checkpoints.body: Move the outcome slider fully right. What changes, and does B's credit appear before, after, or with A's debit?

checkpoints.title: The impossible read
checkpoints.body: Could any reader ever see A = 100 while B still reads 50? Say what the all-or-nothing rule forbids.

checkpoints.title: Abort
checkpoints.body: Move the slider fully left. What happens to the staged 100, and what do A and B read now?

checkpoints.title: Not speed
checkpoints.body: In one sentence: is atomic about how fast the transfer runs, or about which states other sessions are allowed to see?

narration.text: Account A holds 200 and B holds 50. The transaction stages a debit of 100 on A and a credit of 100 on B.
The buffer is private. The committed table, which other sessions read, still shows 200 and 50.
Commit applies both staged writes as one unit: A becomes 100 and B becomes 150, with no readable moment in between.
Rollback discards the buffer instead. The committed values never moved, so no partial debit can survive.
Atomicity is all-or-nothing, not speed: it is a rule about which states other sessions can ever observe.

fallback.text: Static two-column table. The committed column shows A = 200 and B = 50, which is what every other session reads. The private buffer shows a staged debit A = 100 and B = 50, not yet credited. If the transaction commits, both committed values change together to A = 100 and B = 150; if it aborts, the buffer is discarded and the committed values stay 200 and 50. No reader ever sees A = 100 together with B = 50. Caption: atomicity means the two writes are one unit; it is not a claim about speed.

accessibility.alt: A table with two columns and two rows. The left column is the committed table visible to every session, with A = 200 and B = 50. The right column is the transaction's private buffer, holding a staged debit A = 100 and B = 50 before the credit is written. A three-position outcome slider moves from abort through in flight to commit: moving it right changes both committed values together to A = 100 and B = 150, while the buffer disappears; moving it left discards the buffer and leaves A = 200 and B = 50. A banner names the chosen outcome, and notes explain that other sessions read only the committed column.
